title: Later-born generations have better memory and lose it more slowly - Nature Medicine
html:
Dementia risk at any age has been falling for decades. An analysis of ~219,000 people followed for up to 30 years shows that newer generations start old age with a larger cognitive capacity that declines more slowly than that of previous generations, and this combined advantage is large enough to account for the fall in dementia incidence.

References

  • Wolters, F. J. et al. Twenty-seven-year time trends in dementia incidence in Europe and the United States. Neurology 95, 519–531 (2020). This meta-analysis of seven population-based cohorts documents a 13% per-decade fall in dementia incidence.

  • Bratsberg, B., Fjell, A. M., Rogeberg, O. & Walhovd, K. B. Educational expansion and the hidden reversal of the Flynn effect — differential trends across socioeconomic strata. Proc. Natl Acad. Sci. USA 123, e2536089123 (2026). This article documents the reversal of the Flynn effect in Norwegian population data, demonstrating that generational cognitive gains rise and fall with changing societal conditions.

  • Nyberg, L., Lovden, M., Riklund, K., Lindenberger, U. & Backman, L. Memory aging and brain maintenance. Trends Cogn. Sci. 16, 292–305 (2012). This article introduces the brain-maintenance framework, in which preserved brain integrity underlies preserved cognition in aging.

  • Livingston, G. et al. Dementia prevention, intervention, and care: 2024 report of the Lancet standing Commission. Lancet 404, 572–628 (2024). This most recent Lancet Commission report enumerates modifiable dementia risk factors and assigns them to different life stages.

  • Walhovd, K. B., Lovden, M. & Fjell, A. M. Timing of lifespan influences on brain and cognition. Trends Cogn. Sci. 27, 901–915 (2023). This perspective argues that influences on late-life brain and cognition often originate decades earlier, a theoretical foundation of the present study.
